stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD EASES TO 5.27% BUT HOLDS NEAR TWO-DECADE HIGH AS FED STAYS IN HIKING MODE
stories.body: The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield slipped 4 bps to 5.27%, pulling back modestly from last month's highest level since 2007 after the Fed's mid-September hike lifted the fed funds rate to a 3.75%-4% range. The 10-year is still up more than 110 bps year-to-date as investors demand extra compensation for a deteriorating inflation outlook.
stories.explain: The Fed hiked instead of cutting because the current inflation shock is being driven by an oil-supply disruption out of the Strait of Hormuz, not excess demand — and a central bank facing a supply shock has to choose between accommodating higher prices or raising rates to keep the shock from spreading into wages and long-run inflation expectations, which the University of Michigan survey put at 4.6% in September, the highest since June. Today's pullback in yields reflects markets pricing a real chance the hike is enough to anchor those expectations, but the move is happening at the term-premium level — the extra yield investors demand for duration risk — rather than through a change in near-term growth expectations.

stories.headline: S&P 500 HITS 7,819, NASDAQ-100 TOPS 31,200 AS AI MEGA-CAPS EXTEND RECORD RUN DESPITE 5%-PLUS YIELDS
stories.body: The S&P 500 climbed 0.58% to 7,819 and the Nasdaq-100 added 0.48% to 31,224, both fresh records, as mega-cap AI names continued to absorb a 10-year yield still above 5% without missing a step.
stories.explain: Equities decoupling from a historically high discount rate works when an index's biggest constituents generate enough free cash flow that higher borrowing costs barely touch them — names like Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta don't need to roll over debt to fund capex the way a rate-sensitive homebuilder or regional bank does. That's why the rally keeps concentrating in the same handful of balance-sheet-rich names rather than broadening into the sectors that would actually benefit from the Fed eventually cutting.

stories.headline: OIL HOLDS NEAR $90 AS HORMUZ RISK PREMIUM FADES; GOLD PUSHES TOWARD $4,200 ON STICKY INFLATION BID
stories.body: WTI crude was roughly flat near $90, down from a post-Hormuz-closure spike above $93 last week, as tanker traffic through the strait showed signs of stabilizing. Gold rose 0.95% to $4,194, within reach of its recent record, as investors keep using it as an inflation hedge even with yields elevated.
stories.explain: Oil's retreat and gold's advance are consistent with the same underlying story: markets are treating the supply shock as easing even as the inflation it already generated gets priced in as sticky. Gold normally struggles when nominal yields are this high because it pays no coupon, but when the inflation-expectations component of the real yield rises as fast as the nominal yield itself, gold's opportunity cost barely changes — which is why it keeps grinding higher alongside a 5%-plus 10-year.

stories.headline: DOLLAR INDEX SLIPS TO 101.85 AS HAVEN FLOWS EASE OFF THEIR RECENT PEAK
stories.body: The DXY fell 0.28% to 101.85, giving back some of its recent climb to an 18-month high, as the acute phase of the European fiscal scare that had driven dollar buying showed signs of calming.
stories.explain: The dollar's recent strength was a relative-safety trade, not a vote of confidence in the U.S. economy specifically — capital was fleeing French and broader European sovereign risk toward the deepest, most liquid alternative, which is still Treasuries and dollars, even with U.S. yields already near two-decade highs. As that acute stress eases, some of those flows unwind, which is why the dollar can soften even though nothing has really improved about the U.S. fiscal or inflation picture.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S LOSES GUARD DONNIE FREEMAN FOR THE SEASON TO ACHILLES INJURY BEFORE TIP-OFF
stories.body: Rising junior guard Donnie Freeman underwent surgery for a non-contact Achilles injury suffered in a team workout, ruling him out for the entire 2026-27 season before it even begins. Coach Rick Pitino confirmed the injury directly, calling it a major blow to the Red Storm's depth heading into Big East play, which tips off in November.

stories.headline: LAKERS' REPORTED $12 BILLION SALE HEADLINES NBA PRESEASON AS LEBRON DEBUTS WITH SIXERS
stories.body: A reported $12 billion sale of the Lakers — a North American sports franchise record — is the backdrop to a 67-game preseason slate now underway league-wide. LeBron James opened his 24th season with his fourth franchise after signing with Philadelphia, pairing with Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid, and Tyrese Maxey, while the Thunder and Pelicans play a preseason game in Tulsa tonight.

stories.headline: FALCONS' JAMES PEARCE JR. SUSPENDED 8 GAMES FOR CONDUCT POLICY VIOLATION
stories.body: Atlanta edge rusher James Pearce Jr. was suspended eight games without pay for violating the NFL's personal-conduct policy, a significant loss for the Falcons' pass rush. The move comes as the league rolls out its midseason "NFL Top 100" rankings, with Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold climbing 51 spots to No. 21.

stories.headline: OHIO STATE'S JEREMIAH SMITH SETS PROGRAM RECORDS AS ALABAMA, MISSOURI DELIVER THE WEEKEND'S BIGGEST ROAD WINS
stories.body: Ohio State receiver Jeremiah Smith broke the program's career receptions and touchdown records with 11 catches for 206 yards and two scores in a 31-14 win over Iowa, while No. 7 Alabama's 56-23 rout of Mississippi State and No. 25 Missouri's 45-17 upset of No. 8 Florida were the weekend's signature results. Georgia, Texas, and Notre Dame sit 1-2-3 in the latest national rankings.

sports.detail: Fell to 3-1 (0-1 Big Ten) in a road loss at No. 18 USC Saturday. Punter Hunter Green was named to the Ray Guy Award's "Ray's 8" for Week Five. Next: host No. 20 Iowa at Husky Stadium Friday, Oct. 9 — the Hawkeyes' first trip to Montlake in 63 years.

Added former Oregon assistant Mike Mennenga to the staff and brought in six transfers to pair with returning starter Wesley Yates III. First look comes in an exhibition at Boise State Oct. 17, before hosting rival Washington State Oct. 25 — the first-ever October meeting in the 110-year rivalry, with no regular-season game this year.

deepDive.title: Why the Fed Hiked Into an Oil Shock Instead of Cutting
content: Today's brief has the Fed funds rate sitting at 3.75%-4% after a September hike, the 10-year Treasury yield easing only slightly to 5.27% — still near its highest level since 2007 — and WTI crude holding near $90 after a Strait of Hormuz-driven spike above $93. That combination looks backwards next to the textbook playbook: a central bank facing an energy shock and fragile growth normally cuts rates to cushion the economy. Instead, the Fed raised them. Understanding why requires separating two very different kinds of inflation and recognizing which one policymakers are actually worried about right now.

Demand-pull inflation comes from an overheating economy — too much spending chasing too few goods — and the Fed's main tool, raising rates to cool borrowing and spending, works directly on it. Cost-push inflation, like an oil-supply disruption from a closed Hormuz chokepoint, is different: higher rates can't produce more oil or reopen a shipping lane, so hiking does nothing to fix the actual shortage. What hiking can do is prevent that one-time price shock from becoming permanent, by raising borrowing costs enough to slow overall demand and signal that the Fed won't tolerate the shock spreading into wages, rents, and every other price in the economy.

What most casual observers miss is that the Fed isn't really targeting today's price level — it's targeting expectations about tomorrow's. The University of Michigan survey showing year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.6% matters more to policymakers than the current CPI print, because once households and businesses expect higher inflation, they build it into wage demands and price-setting, which then validates the expectation and makes it self-fulfilling. The precedent is 1979-80: Paul Volcker's Fed hiked aggressively straight through the second oil shock of that decade, deliberately inducing a recession, specifically to break an inflation psychology that had already taken hold after a decade of accommodation.

That history is exactly why the 10-year yield, not just the Fed funds rate, is the number worth watching this week. A 5.27% long-term yield embeds the market's own judgment about whether the Fed's hike will be enough to hold expectations in place; it's priced through a term premium that rises when investors doubt that judgment. The next CPI print and the next University of Michigan survey are the real tests: an expectations reading that keeps climbing above 4.6% would argue the Fed has to go further, pushing yields — and mortgage and corporate borrowing costs — even higher, while a stabilizing read would validate the hike as sufficient and open the door to the yield relief markets are already betting on today.
